name: Great Mosque of Djenné
info: The Great Mosque of Djenné is a mosque of sun-baked earth brick in the Sudano-Sahelian style, standing in Djenné, Mali; a first mosque was built there around the 13th century and the present building dates from 1907.

facts.made: A first mosque of uncertain date, later rebuilt more than once; the present building was raised in 1907 by Djenné's guild of masons under its head, Ismaila Traoré, using forced labour
facts.form: Sun-baked earth bricks (ferey) with earth-based mortar and plaster, on a platform about 75 m by 75 m raised 3 metres; a prayer hall about 26 by 50 metres with ninety pillars, and three towers in the qibla wall, the central one around 16 metres high
facts.where: In the city of Djenné, Mali, on the flood plain of the Bani River, beside the town's market square
facts.known: the largest adobe brick building in the world; the three towers of the qibla wall; the toron palm sticks projecting from its walls; the annual festival of replastering; its place on Mali's coat of arms; the 1988 UNESCO listing

t: The date of the first mosque is unknown, with dates from 1200 to 1330 suggested, and the building seen today was rebuilt in 1906 and 1907 in the colonial period.

Historians disagree about the French role in the 1907 design: Félix Dubois blamed the colonial administration, while Jean-Louis Bourgeois argued that the design is basically African and that the local guild of masons built it.
The whole community of Djenné repairs the earth walls each year at a festival, and the town has resisted modernisation of the building in favour of its historical integrity.
dyk: The three towers of the qibla wall are topped with cone-shaped pinnacles crowned with ostrich eggs, and the bundles of palm sticks that stud the walls double as built-in scaffolding for the yearly repairs.
ev: A first mosque was built on the site, on dates that range from 1200 to 1330 in different suggestions
The French explorer René Caillié visited Djenné and found the mosque in ruin, its court used for prayer
Seku Amadu began a new, low mosque without towers or ornament to the east of the old one, finished by 1836
French forces led by Louis Archinard captured Djenné
The original mosque was rebuilt using forced labour under Ismaila Traoré, after the town arranged it in 1906
An inexact replica, the Missiri mosque, was built in cement at Fréjus in southern France
The historic areas of Djenné, including the Great Mosque, were designated a World Heritage Site by UNESCO
The upper section of the large southern tower collapsed after heavy rain, and the Aga Khan Trust for Culture funded its rebuilding

sections.origins:
The Great Mosque stands in the city of Djenné, Mali, on the flood plain of the Bani River. The actual date of construction of the first mosque is unknown: dates as early as 1200 and as late as 1330 have been suggested. The earliest document to mention it is Abd al-Sadi's Tarikh al-Sudan, which gives the early history, presumably from the oral tradition as it existed in the mid-seventeenth century. The Tarikh states that a Sultan Kunburu became a Muslim at the end of the 6th century of the hijra, around 1200, and had his palace pulled down and the site turned into a mosque. He built another palace for himself near the mosque, on the east side. His immediate successor built the towers of the mosque, and the following Sultan built the surrounding wall.

The architectural historian Labelle Prussin presents a more recent interpretation. In her account the mosque built by Koy Kounboro was razed by his successor Malaha Tampo, who built a new one, and the Songhay ruler Askia Mohammed later rebuilt the original mosque of Koy Kounboro, at the end of the 15th century. The original mosque presided over one of the most important Islamic centres of learning in Africa during the Middle Ages, with thousands of students coming to study the Quran in Djenné's madrasas.
sections.content:
The walls are made of sun-baked earth bricks, called ferey, laid with a sand and earth-based mortar and coated with a plaster that gives the building its smooth, sculpted look. Bundles of rodier palm sticks, called toron, project about 60 cm from the walls, and ceramic half-pipes extend from the roofline to direct rain water away from them. The building stands on a platform of about 75 m by 75 m, raised 3 metres above the marketplace so that the Bani's floods do not damage it, and reached by six sets of stairs. The main entrance is on the north side, and the outer walls are not precisely orthogonal, so that the plan is noticeably trapezoidal.

The prayer wall, or qibla, faces east towards Mecca and overlooks the market. It is dominated by three large, box-like towers, the central one around 16 metres high, and strengthened on the outside by eighteen pilaster-like buttresses, each topped by a pinnacle. The prayer hall, about 26 by 50 metres, occupies the eastern half of the mosque. Nine interior walls pierced by pointed arches create a forest of ninety massive pillars, and small windows let little light in. Each tower holds a mihrab, and the imam leads prayers from the central one; beside it is the minbar, from which he preaches the Friday sermon. A courtyard of 20 m by 46 m lies to the west, with galleries on three sides, the western one reserved for women.
sections.making:
In 1906 the town arranged for the original mosque to be rebuilt and for a school to be constructed on the site of Seku Amadu's mosque. The rebuilding was completed in 1907, using forced labour under the direction of Ismaila Traoré, head of Djenné's guild of masons. Photographs taken at the time suggest that the position of at least some of the outer walls follows those of the original mosque, but it is unclear whether the columns supporting the roof kept the previous arrangement. What was almost certainly new was the symmetric arrangement of three large towers in the qibla wall.

There has been debate about how far French influence shaped the design, although it is unlikely that French engineers worked on the building at all. Jean-Louis Bourgeois recorded that the rebuilt mosque was constructed by the traditional local guild of masons, who were responsible for the town's original mosque and its other buildings, using traditional techniques and with minimal French involvement. He argued that the French had little influence, except perhaps for the internal arches, and that the design is basically African. Most of the city's inhabitants, including the Islamic elite who had been harassed by Seku Amadu and humiliated by the destruction of the old mosque, wanted an exact rebuilding of the old mosque in their own vision.
sections.reception:
After the Tarikh al-Sudan there is no written information on the mosque until the French explorer René Caillié visited Djenné in 1828, years after it had been allowed to fall into ruin. He wrote that it was a mosque built of earth, surmounted by two massive but not high towers, rudely constructed though very large, and abandoned to thousands of swallows, so that prayers had come to be said in a small outer court to avoid the smell.

The French journalist Félix Dubois visited soon after the capture of Djenné in 1893 and described the ruins, whose interior was then used as a cemetery. When he returned in 1910 he was shocked by the reconstructed mosque. He believed that the French colonial administration was responsible for the design, and wrote that it looked like a cross between a hedgehog and a church organ. The French ethnologist Michel Leiris, travelling through Mali in 1931, stated that the new mosque was the work of Europeans, and that local people were so unhappy with it that they refused to clean it until threatened with prison. Bourgeois, by contrast, recorded that it was built by the town's masons.
sections.survival:
Prussin's account holds that the Songhay mosque was destroyed again at the Moroccan invasion at the end of the 16th century, and that the one the Tarikh refers to was then rebuilt. Ten years before Caillié's visit the Fulani leader Seku Amadu had launched his jihad and conquered the town. He appears to have disapproved of the existing mosque and allowed it to fall into disrepair, and he closed all the small neighbourhood mosques. Between 1834 and 1836 he built a new mosque to the east of the old one, on the site of the former palace: a large, low building lacking any towers or ornamentation.

The mosque has needed continual repair. On 20 January 2006 the sight of men hacking at the roof, inspecting it for a restoration project financed by the Aga Khan Trust for Culture, sparked a riot in the town in which one man died. On 5 November 2009 the upper section of the southern large tower of the qibla wall collapsed after 75 mm of rain fell in a 24-hour period, and the Aga Khan Trust for Culture funded its rebuilding. Since 1907 only small changes have been made to the design: the mihrab tower originally had a pair of large recesses instead of a single niche, and two additional rows of toron were added to the walls in the early 1990s.
sections.legacy:
The entire community of Djenné takes an active part in the mosque's maintenance during an annual festival, with music and food, to repair the damage of the past year, mostly erosion caused by the annual rains and cracks caused by changes in temperature and humidity. Plaster is prepared in pits, men climb the palm-wood scaffolding and ladders to smear it over the walls, a race opens the festival to see who first delivers plaster to the mosque, and women and girls carry water. Members of the masons' guild direct the work.

Electrical wiring and plumbing have been added to many mosques in Mali, in some cases with the original surfaces tiled over. The Great Mosque has been equipped with a loudspeaker system, but the citizens of Djenné have resisted modernisation in favour of its historical integrity, and many preservationists have praised their effort. The historic areas of Djenné, including the mosque, were designated a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1988, and the mosque is the most prominent symbol of both the city and the nation of Mali; it features on Mali's coat of arms. In 1930 an inexact replica, the Missiri mosque, was built in cement at Fréjus in southern France for the West African colonial troops of the French Army. The Zamani Project documented the mosque in 3D with laser scanning in 2005.

summary: The Great Mosque of Djenné in Mali is the largest adobe brick building in the world. A first mosque stood there from about the 13th century; the present building was raised in 1907 by the town's masons and is replastered every year by the whole community. UNESCO listed it in 1988.
references: S. Schutyser, Banco, Adobe Mosques of the Inner Niger Delta (5 Continents Editions, 2003)
notes: Start date: the article says the first mosque's date is unknown, suggested between 1200 and 1330; 1200 used with circa true. The present building is 1907.
The article contradicts itself on the later date of the new mosque: 1907 in the lead and Present mosque section, 1909 in Prussin's account. 1909 left out.

Prussin says Sheku Ahmadu in 1830 removed the old roof timbers and built a more austere structure on the site of the Kounboro mosque; the History section says Seku Amadu built a new mosque in 1834-1836 to the east, on the former palace site. The 1830 account was left out.
The article spells the Fulani leader Seku Amadu and Sheku Ahmadu; Seku Amadu used.
Left out: the film and video game mentions, and the 'Notes' stub.
Hedgehog quotation: kept only the hedgehog and church organ phrase; Dubois's further remark was left out.
